title: Any PSS Super experts here?
body:
O.P.
I'm hoping for some feedback for anyone that knows the PSS Super scheme well.
It seems to me that for anyone that's been in the PSS for 20+ years and has few promotional prospects, they would be far better off preserving their PSS benefit, and changing to PSSap (or other schemes). The reason is that if you stay in PSS, you'll get little growth per year... all you can get is a 0.31 added to your multiple, which does not growth your overall benefit much if you've already got a decent multiple. However if you preserve your PSS, it still continues to grow (employer benefit at CPI, employee at Fund Growth), while in addition the Goverment will contribute 15.4% to your nominated fund. If you continue to contribute 10% of your salary (that you contributed to PSS before), you can now salary sacrifise this to PSSap.
When you're ready to retire, your PSS pension may be a little different (more or less) than if you had stayed in the PSS, but you'll end up with a significant lump sum in PSSap.
Seems almost too good to be true. Have I missed anything here?
Thanks for any feedback!

---- replies ----
[User #9765222 postsAlfieForum Regular] Is it possible to preserve a PSS and change over to PSSap? I thought it was one or the other. My understanding was once you preserve your PSS, you wont be able to contribute to it. Wouldn't the multiple increase with the length of time in the PSS and in-turn increase the PSS pension?
I have been in the PSS for 12 years now and contribute 10% to get the .31 multiple.
[User #2407553195 postsBetheBallDig up stupid!!!Whirlpool Forums Addict] this post was edited
PSS is way way way better than pssap. PSS is a defined index pension for life. The higher that multiple the more you get for the rest of your life. Never take a lump sum out if this one. Pssap, will run out! It's that simple.... However if you get to your max multiple, usually 10, for the pss, then you start in the pssap.
Edit: but if you can afford 10%, extra for pssap and have no mortgage, go for it.
[User #2407553195 postsBetheBallDig up stupid!!!Whirlpool Forums Addict] Alfie writes...
Is it possible to preserve a PSS and change over to PSSap?
I'm pretty sure you can have both going. You can put 0 into the PSS and the multiple still grows by 0.11. At 5%, it's 0.21 at 10%, as you know, it's 0.31.
Op, at 20+ years give them a call. They have financial planners that are experts in the PSS and charge a once off fee that isn't tied into anything.
OP, what's your multiple?.... Nearing 10? At an end super salary of $100000 for argument sake, each multiple step is about $8000 ish less per year..... Indexed. Eg $100000 / 12 x 10 (multi) = $83333. At 9 (multi) = $75000... And so on.
[User #6219341960 postsfamilywithkidsWhirlpool Enthusiast] O.P.
Alfie: Yes, since 2008 you can change. In the early years PSS is very generous, but as your multiple grows, your total lump sum growth slows down a lot. Say for example your multiple is 6 and ave salary is $100,000. The growth of your lump sum over a year is only 1-(6.31/6)=5.2%. Work it out, you'll see that this right. When the multiple is low, the growth is MUCH higher.
BetheBall: I think you're missing the point. To get the better benefit you must preserve the PSS completely, which means you keep the full balance in there, and it continues grow even though you make no more contributions into it (employer component growths at CPI, employee at Fund Growth). You can still take this as a full pension when you retire. However you must leave the PSS (and preserving the full benefit) and change FUTURE contribution to PSSap, to get the government to put in their 15.4%, which is ON TOP of your salary. So you still end up with a fully indexed pension, plus an additional lump sum which is payed for by the 15.4% that the government contributes. You can salary sacrifise in more to grow it further.
[User #5249165682 postsjhauWhirlpool Forums Addict] familywithkids writes...
I'm hoping for some feedback for anyone that knows the PSS Super scheme well.
I don't know that much about it, but I do know that the PSS is superior to the PSSap.
As others have noted, the PSS is a defined-benefit scheme. If you're a member for long enough, and if you contribute more than the required amount (ie increase your contributions), you can effectively retire with a pension equivalent to 100% of your average salary over the two years prior to retirement. Your level of pension is guaranteed regardless of the stock market, regardless of any other fluctuations. It's a gold-plated pension scheme.
Try finding a scheme like that around nowadays – you won't be able to.
If you'd like to branch out, and if you can afford to do so, then up your contributions to the PSS so as to increase your final pension amount, and also contribute via salary sacrifice. I think that the salary sacrificed amounts go into the PSSap, or at least, into an account that's separate to the defined benefit pension account.
[User #21852728839 postsSir Moi of AusJe Suis MoiWhirlpool Forums Addict] bob999 writes...
CSS = Gold PSS = Silver PSSap= Bronze
Succinctly put.
I remember those of us who started just after the CSS closed. Spewing we missed out. But now, we thank our lucky stars we aren't in the PSSap :)
[User #7069621 postsAus ATCI'm new here, please be nice] Don't feel too hard done by in PSS.
With AvSuper defined benefits (which you cannot join any more – like PSS), 5% = 20% accumulation (vs 21%), and above 5% the benefit is calculated (averaged over period of service) at only 1.2% for each % above 5%. At the extreme, if you contribute 10% from day 1, the benefit multiple is 26% (vs 31%) per year.
But we can salary sacrifice to our defined benefit scheme – not sure about PSS.
Don't forget, we not only get the benefit multiple increase, but also the FAS increases each year as well.

[User #21852728839 postsSir Moi of AusJe Suis MoiWhirlpool Forums Addict] Aus ATC writes...
But we can salary sacrifice to our defined benefit scheme – not sure about PSS.
For PSS, no we're not allowed to salary sacrifice into PSS itself.
If PSS members do salary sacrifice, they'll start up an additional account with PSSap instead.
Don't forget, we not only get the benefit multiple increase, but also the FAS increases each year as well.
Some of us will always have a higher FAS than our actual salary as the FAS can't go backwards (thanks higher duties) I know people sometimes complain that in this case, they are paying more than their nominated rate against their actual salary, but it all works out in the end :)
[User #6219341960 postsfamilywithkidsWhirlpool Enthusiast] O.P.
Thanks guys, I do appreciate your responses! However this topic is not about how great the PSS is, and how well it compares to other schemes...I'm already convinced the PSS is a great scheme and I'm lucky to be in it. This topic is about: 'Continuing contributing to PSS' vs 'Preserving PSS and making future contributions to PSSap'.
BetheBall: Yes I've been to several of these seminars already, which has given me a great understanding of how it works. I've also gone through all the documentation in detail, and this enabled me to do all my own calculations. I've also asked PSS questions directly about the scheme and if the option I propose is possible, and all the answers were Yes. I've not gone to see the financial advisors since I don't feel this is their area of expertise. It requires someone with detailed knowledge of how the PSS and PSSap rules work, and what the implications are of a changeover in the way I described. Financially this looks like a no-brainer to me, but I can't help but wonder if there's something I've missed, as the option seems almost too good to be true.

[User #8767613579 postsargamondWhirlpool Forums Addict] the pss offers one of the best pension rates, indexed for life. however, if you believe that you and your spouse will die shortly after retirement, then the pssap would be better
[User #17144152 postsRobForum Regular] On my reading of the pss scheme I believe you are on the right track, however this is largely based on your assumptions for wage growth, cpi and investment earnings and current multiplier.
Depending on the mix of variables you may find that your contributions plus investment earnings is paying for the majority if not all of the increase in your final amount, therefore government isn't paying anything towards the increase however they are guaranteeing pension index for life. Depending on the mix of variables by not contributing anything you may achieve the same increase if cpi and investment earnings go your way, therefore may make sense in accumulating in the pssap. The major risk if investments go backwards you loose out come pension time.
[User #8767613579 postsargamondWhirlpool Forums Addict] familywithkids writes...
I get the PSS pension for both options...please re-read the question.
Unless you have reached your maximum 10x multiplier, you are not maximising the generous pension benefits
The pssap is just like any private super (with the exception of the larger govt contribution) but this in no way compares to the pension benefits of the pss. Considering that nowadays, a lot of elderly seem to easily reach 80, someone on max pss that retires at 60 gets 90% of their annual salary indexed for life (for at least 20+ years, presuming you are healthy)
You are not going to get the equivalent return from preserving the pss and contributing to the pssap
[User #6219341960 postsfamilywithkidsWhirlpool Enthusiast] O.P.
Rob: Thank you! Yes I agree with you completely, you seem to have a good understanding of how it works as well. I agree there is more risk if I preserve, as I'm more exposed to market conditions, but my assumptions have been very conservative, and the preservation option still seems clearly better.
argamond: Thanks for your input, but I don't think you're grasping what I'm proposing. You can reach you maximum pension even if you preserve, as the benefit continues to grow even when you don't contribute. In fact if the market does well, you can easily reach your maximum benefit more quickly. Please read my posts above again, as I think you may have missed the key points.
